data.title: B. M. Szőke: the latest excavations at Blatnohrad (Mosaburg/Zalavár)
data.excerpt: The Hungarian archaeologist Béla Miklós Szőke summarises new insights into Mosaburg/Zalavár – Blatnohrad – the seat of Prince Pribina and his son Koceľ. He describes the Carolingian civitas divided into three parts, the three churches named in the Conversio, and an unusually large pilgrimage church with an outer ring crypt, painted window glass and a glassworking workshop beside its apse.
data.metaDescription: A study by Béla Miklós Szőke on the excavations at Mosaburg/Zalavár, the Blatnohrad of Prince Pribina and his son Koceľ, and on its churches.

children.text: We are bringing our readers something that, as far as I know, has never been published anywhere in Slovakia in Slovak or Czech. With the permission of the Hungarian archaeologist Dr Béla Miklós Szőke, who studies Slavic occupation in the region of Blatnohrad (Zalavár by Lake Balaton), we have prepared a good-quality translation of his scholarly paper, which appeared in English in 2007. In it he summarises exceptionally interesting new insights into the occupation of Blatnohrad in the time of Prince Pribina and his son Koceľ. For the quality of the translation we thank our colleague Robert Spytihnev Michalič.
Béla Miklós Szőke: New finds from the excavations at Mosaburg/Zalavár (Blatnohrad, western Hungary)
The origins of Pribina's and Koceľ's comitatus at Blatnohrad (Mosaburg/Zalavár)
At the end of the eighth century a new stage began in the history of the Carpathian Basin. Between 791 and 811 the Avar Khaganate, the most important power in the east of central Europe,
was subjugated by the Frankish Empire of Charlemagne and its territory was divided into several smaller areas.
Vassal principalities were established on the northern and southern margins of the empire, while the central region west of the Danube was incorporated directly into the Frankish Empire.
The population of the former khaganate in the areas east of the Danube, although politically neutral, probably fell under the indirect rule of the Frankish Empire.

Pannonia, that is, the eastern territory of the empire, was divided into several comitatus, which served as smaller administrative units. One such comitatus was created along the upper Danube; another lay in the region of Sabaria/Szombathely.
But a further comitatus with its seat at Mosaburg/Zalavár

(Blatnohrad) was founded at a relatively late date, along the river Zala in Lower Pannonia, by Pribina, the former duke of Nitra, and his son Koceľ. The most important events of this comitatus up to the year 870 are recorded in detail in the Conversio Bagoariorum et Carantanorum (hereafter only Conversio).

The information contained in this account and the finds from the excavations carried out over the last 50 years at the seat of the comitatus allow us to undertake a new analysis and a new interpretation of the cultural contacts of the population living here, and a better understanding of certain buildings at Mosaburg/Zalavár/Blatnohrad.
The cultural environment of the population at Mosaburg/Zalavár/Blatnohrad
When Pribina settled at Mosaburg in the early 840s, he “gathered people from all around”.
Part of this population can be identified as Avar-Slavic groups living in this area since the seventh century, which had a distinctly mixed culture known as the Pókaszepetk–Zalakomár group.

One clearly recognisable feature of this group is the biritual burial rite: the Slavs cremated their dead, while the Avars practised inhumation. The archaeological finds also point to a rich diversity: the costume shows the presence of Slavic, Avar and West Germanic elements, and the pottery found in the settlements suggests the use of both Slavic and Avar products.

Even at the beginning of the ninth century the ethnic differences between the various population groups were reflected in burial customs and costume. On the other hand, certain items of jewellery, implements and tools of everyday life are not specific to any of the cultures named, but are “imperial” in their essence. These products were made in bulk in workshops resembling manufactories and show strong Carolingian influences.
This tendency towards homogeneity grew stronger after the 840s, and evidence of it can be found in finds that are distributed across all social strata.

The shift in social relations that led to the emergence of a new, early feudal aristocracy also affected the products of the various crafts – craftsmen had to meet the demands of the individual ruling family courts and their retinues, producing a wide range of weapons and spurs as well as striking silver and gold jewellery and objects carved from antler. The finds of the so-called “Byzantine-Oriental” horizon (translator's note: this is an artistic style inspired by Byzantine-Oriental art) were at first interpreted as finds representing the type of artefact characteristic of the Great Moravian empire,
while the distribution of this type was interpreted as a reflection of the expansion of Great Moravia at the time of its greatest territorial extent.
(“Greater Moravia”)

But the growing number of finds of jewellery and other artefacts of everyday life of this type within the territory of the Mosaburg/Zalavár (Blatnohrad) comitatus clearly indicates that this find horizon is best interpreted as expressing social rather than ethnic and cultural relations, since this comitatus was never part of the Moravian principality (figure 1) Despite the strong tendency towards cultural assimilation to the west (westernisation) and towards homogeneity from the middle of the ninth century onwards, the rich diversity of Pannonian culture should not be forgotten, a diversity it owes to the different ethnic backgrounds of the people called together “from all around”. The influence of the Bulgar culture of the Danube basin (Danubian Bulgar origin) can be seen in the artificially deformed skull in a male grave,
in certain shapes of pottery and decoration, in the signs and symbols incised on bricks,
as well as in the very well known and popular so-called grape-cluster earrings.
The Byzantine sword found here probably also reached Blatnohrad through these Danubian Bulgars.
Further cultural influences can be seen in items of jewellery, such as the earrings and finger rings of the phases designated Vor-Köttlach and Köttlach I,
as well as in the ornaments and artefacts of everyday life that were widely used in Moravia.

For one particular burial rite involving cremation in a so-called house of the dead, documented in the area of Mosaburg/Zalavár (Blatnohrad), the best parallels are to be found among the north-western Slavs (for example the Sorbs

). In summary, we may say that the cultural diversity of the Pannonian comitatus in the ninth century reflects the diversity of the regions east of Charlemagne's Frankish Empire, from the Baltic to the Pontus.
Civitas Priwinae – Pribina's “city”

The fortifications of Mosaburg were investigated by Géza Fehér in the early 1950s. In his view the entire island was surrounded by a wall constructed by packing earth between two parallel lines of wooden posts linked by wattle.
The remains of a palisade of sessile oak running from north to south were uncovered by Ágnes Cs. Sós.
More recently a ditch roughly 2.5 metres deep and 12 metres wide was uncovered, which crossed the “neck” of the island in an L shape, running from west to east.
The palisade wall running from north to south continued westwards beyond this ditch. It appears that the Carolingian civitas was divided into three parts.

The southern third, south of the ditch and the walls, was inhabited by Pribina's and Koceľ's court and can be identified with the munimen described in the Conversio. The church dignitaries and priests lived in the northern part of the island, in an enclosure similarly surrounded by a palisade. The archbishop of Salzburg and his retinue were accommodated in this enclosure during his visits. East of these two courts lies an area as yet uninvestigated, which probably functioned as a kind of enclosure and provided space for the houses of craftsmen and merchants or for the fortified residences of Pribina's and Koceľ's followers. The excavations revealed that the inhabitants of this civitas lived in large buildings of several rooms built on posts (translator's note: so-called náklonnice) and not in sunken houses typical of rural settlements of this period. Working pits, storage pits, wells, ovens and the like were scattered around these houses.
The churches of Mosaburg/Zalavár/Blatnohrad

The Conversio mentions three churches at Mosaburg. The first lay infra munimen Priwinae. This church, dedicated to Saint Mary, the Mother of God, was consecrated by Liupram, archbishop of Salzburg, on 24 January AD 850.

The second church, infra civitatem, in which the martyr Hadrian was buried (in qua ecclesia Adrianus martyr humatus pausat) and which was therefore exceptionally suited to veneration, was built on Liupram's initiative.
The third church, in eadem civitate, was dedicated to Saint John the Baptist.
Altogether, under the rule of Pribina and Koceľ (c. 850–870), 28 churches were built outside the “city” (foric civitatem), each of them consecrated by successive archbishops of Salzburg.

Only these three churches, however, have been excavated. The ground plan of a fourth church is known to us thanks to an ink drawing by Giulio Turco. The locations and identifications of the various places and churches mentioned in the written sources are unfortunately uncertain.
Zalavár-Vársziget: the church on Giulio Turco's ink drawing (figure 2)

On the evidence of the drawing made by the military engineering officer Giulio Turco in 1569, a three-aisled church with a semicircular apse measuring c. 22.5–24 metres × 9–10 metres stood in the southern part of the island. It lay north of the monastery of the Árpád period, which was rebuilt as a frontier fortress during the Ottoman period. This building was completely destroyed in the last few centuries. Today there is a sand quarry on the site of the church and the later fortress.

Excavations carried out between 1951 and 1954, east and north of the presumed position of the church, brought to light a cemetery with several layers of graves. The character of the graves suggested that they were originally part of a cemetery belonging to the church. The earliest graves (graves with large coffins) can be dated to the middle of the ninth century, while the later graves belong to the Árpád period.
The exact position of the former church cannot be determined for lack of archaeological evidence, and the grave finds do not indicate continuous use of the burial ground during the tenth century.

The church on Giulio Turco's drawing can most probably be identified with the Benedictine church dedicated to Saint Hadrian, which is associated with the monastery founded by the holy king Stephen I in 1019. This church, however, is not identical with the church dedicated to Saint Hadrian that is mentioned in the Conversio. In the ninth century there was a difference between civitas and munimen, since the munimen is described as Pribina's and Koceľ's court in the southern part of the island, and this church can therefore be identified with the one that was dedicated to Saint Mary in the ninth century and later, during the Árpád period, re-consecrated as the church of Saint Hadrian.
Zalavár-Vársziget: a pilgrimage church with an outer ring crypt (figure 3)

In the early 1980s Ágnes Cs. Sós uncovered the foundations of an unusually large church, measuring roughly 50 metres × 24 metres, in the middle of the island. Very little of this church, however, had survived. Only the foundation trenches below the former floor level could be identified. The documentation of the surviving remains was not entirely precise, and so the records of Cs. Sós's excavation did not allow an exact reconstruction of the church's ground plan.

In 1999–2000, therefore, I carried out a check excavation in order to clarify the ground plan of this church. The still surviving remains of the foundation wall and the interior of the church were uncovered and the remains documented in detail. The result of this work was a reconstruction of the church on its original site. The three-aisled church had a semicircular apse. The outer ring crypt lay beyond the apse wall. The so-called “narthex” lay to the west, and probably also a monastery with a square courtyard flanked by two buildings. A round bell tower stood by the western entrance. Inside the semicircular ambulatory crypt there were three chapels and four family crypts. The other family crypts lay along the northern and southern sides of the church. A stone reliquary grave was found beneath the sanctuary. The foundation pits of the wooden posts of an earlier building were uncovered beneath the “narthex”. Ágnes Cs. Sós interpreted them as the remains of a wooden church.

Although little has survived of the interior of the basilica, the few finds that have been brought to light are quite remarkable. Fragments recovered from the wide ditch that protected Pribina's munimen suggest that the basilica had a floor made of a material resembling terrazzo set in mortar.
A simple, undecorated sandstone capital of block form found in the same ditch probably adorned one of the church's columns (figure 4).

Fragments of coloured plaster were found in the fill of the graves. One of the graves contained a few floor tiles with an incised interlace pattern. Further evidence for the decoration of the church's interior consists, on the one hand, of finds of fragments of painted and stained glass window panes depicting Christ and various saints and angels, and, on the other, of some letters. These fragments were found beneath the brick paving of the crypt surrounding the sanctuary (figure 5).

The character and type of the fragments on which a figural scene was painted suggest that they were either part of the decoration of some fenestella or of a richly decorated reliquary casket, while the fragments of coloured glass probably come from the window panes of the church. The remains of a glassworking workshop, where these glass panes were also made, were uncovered not far from the apse of the church.
It appears to me that this church had only a single architectural period and that it was a pilgrimage church
built for the veneration of martyrs.
Its purpose
was the same as that of similar contemporary churches in Saxony, Thuringia and Bavaria.
It was believed that the saints buried in these churches would, with God's help, perform various miracles and so attract many people whose faith would thereby be strengthened.

Such an imposing church could only have been built by a wealthy and powerful person, and it seems reasonable to assume that this person was none other than Liupram, archbishop of Salzburg. The church can thus be identified as the one which, according to the Conversio, was built infra civitatem Priwinae between 850-854 and 859 and in which the “martyr Hadrian was laid to eternal rest” around AD 870.

A cemetery used over several periods extended around the church. The earliest graves date to approximately the middle of the ninth century, the latest to the beginning of the tenth century. By the time the Árpád period arrived, only the ruins of the church remained. The graves of this late period, lying beside the southern side of the church, can be related to the church that lay a little way to the south. This church, dedicated to Saint Mary in the ninth century, was re-consecrated at the beginning of the eleventh century as the church of Saint Hadrian.
The church at Zalavár-Récéskút

The three-aisled stone basilica was investigated by Aladár Radnóti in 1946, 1947 and 1953, and after him also by Ágnes Cs. Sós in 1961 and 1963. The rectangular basilica with three semicircular apses recessed into its wall, built on a sandy island north of Zalavár-Vársziget, measured 20.2–20.5 metres × 12.1 metres. According to Aladár Radnóti, four architectural periods can be distinguished (figure 6).

The first period falls in the ninth century AD, during which it was a single-nave basilica with three apses, a narthex and a baptistery. The terrazzo floor in the apses lay slightly higher than the stone floor of the nave. The walls of the apses were painted. The church could be entered through a southern and a western doorway. The first church burnt down in the ninth century and was rebuilt in its second period either shortly afterwards or only later, in the eleventh century. The nave was divided into three aisles by two rows of columns.
The third and fourth architectural periods represent the late Middle Ages.

Ágnes Cs. Sós noted that Aladár Radnóti's documentation recorded several foundation pits for posts whose function was unclear. She therefore carried out a check excavation to determine their function (figure 7).

On the basis of the finds from her excavation she reconstructed two further architectural periods. The first sacred building on this site was a wooden church, of which very little survived; its dimensions could be reconstructed only approximately from the graves that lay around the building. It appears that the wooden church had roughly the same dimensions as the later stone basilica. The second church could be reconstructed from finds of stone and brick fragments recovered from level “R”, which was cut through by the foundation pits dug for posts (with 2-metre gaps between them) belonging to a further building. This timber and stone basilica was a large, three-aisled building measuring 30 metres × 19.5 metres. Ágnes Cs. Sós assumed that the first church, built entirely of wood, was erected at the beginning of the ninth century, while the second church, built of wood and stone, can be dated to the second half of the ninth century. The third church, of basilica type and built entirely of stone, was erected in the eleventh century. A sharp debate about the architectural periods and the dating of the church began immediately after the publication of Ágnes Cs. Sós's excavation report.

The documentation of her excavation suggests, however, that level “R” post-dates the construction of the stone basilica, and the foundation pits of the posts could therefore also be dated to a later period. Sándor Tóth
assumed that the pits were dug to secure scaffolding during the rebuilding of the church at the beginning of the Árpád period.

It seems to me that these posts can better be explained as the remains of a tenth-century building that no longer had any sacred function, especially in view of the controversies surrounding the scaffolding theory (such as the stones found in the pits and the absence of graves of the Árpád period).

It is also unclear to whom this church was dedicated and with which church described in the Conversio it can be identified. Thomas von Bogyay identified it with the church dedicated to Saint John the Baptist on account of the “baptistery”.

But the presence of a “well” in the “baptistery” is not evident, and according to Ágnes Cs. Sós the “well” is better interpreted as the foundation pit of one of the posts of the second, timber-and-stone church.
The opposite view was held by Dezső Dercsényi,
Géza Entz
and Sándor Tóth,

who thought that the church might be identified as the first church of the Árpád period, dedicated to Saint Hadrian. This interpretation, however, is contradicted by the facts that no graves of the Árpád period were found around the church and that we have absolutely no evidence of any building activity during this period. The church dedicated to Saint John the Baptist, which is said to have stood in eadem civitate, must obviously be sought at the site of Zalavár-Vársziget. It follows from the above that the church uncovered at the site of Zalavár-Récéskút cannot be identified with any of the buildings mentioned in the Conversio. It may have been the private church of one of the noble families of Pribina's and Koceľ's retinue, recalling the wooden church uncovered at the site of Zalaszabar-Borjúállás-sziget.
The church at the site of Zalaszabar-Borjúállás-sziget (Figure 8)

The remains of a single-nave hall church with a rectangular sanctuary and a narthex, measuring 17 metres × 7 metres, were uncovered by Róbert Müller in the early 1980s. The wooden church was built in the style of ground-level log construction. The narrow stone wall that separated the sanctuary recess from the nave can probably be interpreted as the foundation for a chancel screen. Altogether 850 graves from various periods were uncovered around the church. The overwhelming majority of these graves, however, date to the ninth century, with only a small proportion belonging to the tenth. The use of the cemetery ended before the beginning of the Árpád period. The church lay in an area surrounded by a palisade, so that one may speak of the fortified court of some nobleman. A wooden building that served as the residence of the nobleman and his family stood by the entrance. Róbert Müller identified this church as the house of worship dedicated to the protomartyr Saint Stephen which, according to the Conversio, belonged to a certain Wittimar and was consecrated by Adalwin, archbishop of Salzburg, in 865.
